response.sql: WITH gender_counts AS (SELECT c.gender AS gender, COUNT(i.invoice_number) AS invoice_count FROM Invoices i JOIN Orders o ON o.order_id = i.order_id JOIN Customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id GROUP BY c.gender), overall AS (SELECT AVG(invoice_count) AS avg_count FROM gender_counts) SELECT AVG(g.invoice_count) AS avg_invoice_count_above_average, AVG(g.invoice_count - o.avg_count) AS avg_excess_over_overall_average FROM gender_counts g CROSS JOIN overall o WHERE g.invoice_count > o.avg_count;

assumptions.assumption: A missing gender means SQL NULL. NULLs form one group under GROUP BY. Empty or blank gender strings are treated as their own separate gender group.
Each invoice is counted once per customer gender, through Invoices to Orders to Customers. Genders with no invoices do not appear and do not enter the plain average.
Gender values are compared as stored, so differently cased values such as 'M' and 'm' are separate groups.

alternatives.interpretation: Treat blank or whitespace-only gender strings as missing, so they fall into the same group as NULL.
alternatives.sql: WITH gender_counts AS (SELECT CASE WHEN TRIM(c.gender) = '' THEN NULL ELSE c.gender END AS gender, COUNT(i.invoice_number) AS invoice_count FROM Invoices i JOIN Orders o ON o.order_id = i.order_id JOIN Customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id GROUP BY CASE WHEN TRIM(c.gender) = '' THEN NULL ELSE c.gender END), overall AS (SELECT AVG(invoice_count) AS avg_count FROM gender_counts) SELECT AVG(g.invoice_count) AS avg_invoice_count_above_average, AVG(g.invoice_count - o.avg_count) AS avg_excess_over_overall_average FROM gender_counts g CROSS JOIN overall o WHERE g.invoice_count > o.avg_count;
